Yes, it is fully funded through 2033. The Trustees Report comes out every summer. Here is the 2014 report.

If a person earning the US median wage were allowed to invest in one of the various well-known market index funds, instead of contributing to Social Security (same amount of contribution though) - what would their account be worth when they reached typical age for retirement?

Who knows? While the stock market has a high average return, that return may not be so high for decades at a time. If you happen to be investing in slow decades, you could be very surprised. SSA always pays the same rate per check.

The stock market acts as a "Defined Contribution Plan." This means you get out of it what you put in plus capital gains, if any. You can lose principle or you can outlive your earnings.

Social Security acts as a "Defined Benefit Plan." You will receive a monthly benefit, with COLAs each year, for the rest of your life no matter how long you live. You also receive a package of insurance benefits that includes disability, survivors, and child benefits, which the stock market simply does not give you.

If the government "allowed" you to invest your money in a stock plan rather than SSA, this would have to be mandatory. That would create a whole big world of problems.
